item.research_question: How does the microstructure and phase stability of an equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn high-entropy alloy evolve during and after selective laser melting (SLM) and subsequent high-temperature annealing, and what is the impact on mechanical properties?
item.material_system: Equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn (Cantor alloy) produced from mechanically alloyed powders (purity >97 at.%)
item.processing_route: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using SISMA MYSINT100 RM with Nitrogen atmosphere (O2 <0.5%), layer thickness H=0.05 mm, energy density F=200 J/mm3, recoating rate 70/150 mm/s, spot diameter 50 μm; followed by cold rolling (90% thickness reduction) and annealing at 723–1423 K for 25 h or 1170 K for 100 h
item.test_conditions: Microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM-FEG-EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness; annealing temperatures: 723, 823, 923, 1023, 1123, 1223, 1323, 1423 K
key_findings: The as-built SLM alloy contains fine Cr-rich nitride and σ phase precipitates despite XRD showing a single FCC structure.
Precipitates increase in number and size after annealing between 900 K and 1300 K, with σ phase nucleating at grain boundaries and triple points.
At 1423 K, the σ phase and most nitrides dissolve, resulting in a single FCC structure with near-equieatomic composition.
Cold rolling followed by annealing accelerates recrystallization and σ phase precipitation compared to as-built samples.
Microhardness increases significantly after cold rolling and at low annealing temperatures (723–823 K) due to fine precipitates.
Hardness decreases progressively above 1023 K as σ phase grows and grains coarsen, following the Hall–Petch relationship.
The σ phase is tetragonal, Cr-rich (~50 at.%), and forms preferentially at grain boundaries and triple points during recrystallization.
item.mechanism: Nitrogen interstitial diffusion during SLM leads to supersaturation and nitride nucleation; subsequent thermal cycles and rapid cooling promote heterogeneous nucleation of σ phase around nitrides. Recrystallization and increased diffusion rates at higher temperatures cause σ phase growth at boundaries, while very high temperatures (≥1423 K) enable dissolution back to a single FCC phase.
item.limitations: The text states that distinguishing between Cr2N and CrN via EDS is difficult due to small precipitate size, and that the exact activation energy for precipitation requires further nucleation and coarsening studies.
item.future_work: Further experimental work focusing on nucleation and coarsening is required to fully understand the precipitation process; thermodynamic databases and models need to be extended to better understand this complex alloy behavior.
quotes: The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K.

Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries.

The size of the σ phase precipitates increased with annealing temperature. When the annealing temperature was below the recrystallization temperature, the size of precipitates was small due to a low diffusion rate and confined at the grain boundaries of the as-built dendritic structure.
